# Storyfolio

Makes one kind of portfolio site: one long scroll that tells one story, carried by one object in 3D that is taken from the person's own work.

This version plans the site and does not build it. It ends when the person has said yes to a storyboard.

## Three stops

Between stops you work by yourself. At each stop the person decides one thing. You go on only when their answer is in the conversation and you have written it into the file.

| Stop | First open | You put to the person | You go on when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Read | `references/reading-a-profile.md` | What you found, as facts to confirm and questions to answer. Nothing else | They have answered, and `docs/story/facts.md` holds their answers |
| 2. Concept | `references/concept.md` | Three concepts, and which you would choose | They have picked one, or told you to pick, and `docs/story/concepts.md` says which |
| 3. Storyboard | `references/storyboard.md` | The script of the whole page | They have said yes to it |

**Your first reply is the first stop, and no more than that.** People ask for the whole plan at once: the idea, the scroll, the colours. Do not give it yet, and say why in a sentence. A plan made now is made from your reading of a resume, and a resume leaves out exactly what a site must not get wrong: whose result a number was, what a title hides, who took a photograph. Once they have answered you will have a better idea, and it will not have to be taken apart.

When the storyboard has its yes, say that building is not in this version, and bring `docs/story/handover.md` up to date.

## Ask or decide

Ask the person when a thing is:

1. a fact only they know,
2. a claim that could embarrass them if it were wrong,
3. taste on what a visitor sees first: the concept, the look, the opening words,
4. anything that publishes, costs money, or shows another person or an employer's work.

Everything else you decide. Write each decision into `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`: what you decided, why, and how to change it.

If the person will not answer, or tells you to decide everything, open `references/asking.md`.

## What you keep

In the person's own folder, so that a later session can go on from the files alone:

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `docs/story/facts.md` | The fact sheet, each fact with where it came from, and the person's answers |
| `docs/story/concepts.md` | The three concepts, which was picked, and why |
| `docs/story/storyboard.md` | The script |
| `docs/story/decided-for-you.md` | What you decided without asking |
| `docs/story/handover.md` | What exists, what the person has said, what is next |

## What holds from the first stop on

- **Nothing about the person is invented.** You know that a number, an employer, a title and a quote are facts. So is a sentence about what was wrong before they came, how often a thing is used, why something happened, or what a project taught them. A sentence like that sounds like writing, and it is a claim. If the fact sheet does not hold it, ask for it or leave it out.
- **A number is used as the person confirmed it,** with what it measures and whose result it is.
- **What is someone else's is asked about before it is planned for:** a photograph a photographer took, a friend's drawing, a quote, an employer's screens, a story with a patient or a client in it.


ARGUMENTS: Plan only, do not build. User wants an award-winning, non-template portfolio with 3D and scroll-driven animation that feels personal. All material is in the "material" folder in the working directory.

Why nurses skip the scan: an observational study of workarounds on one
cardiac ward

A. Brennan, RGN. Irish Nursing Informatics Conference 2025 (poster)

Background. Barcode medication administration only protects patients when
the wristband and the medicine are both scanned. On our ward 29% of doses
were being given without a scan.

Method. Forty hours of observation across day and night shifts, and short
interviews with 22 nurses.

Findings. Three workarounds accounted for most missed scans: wristbands that
would not scan after a shower, scanners kept on a trolley away from the
medication room, and scanning from a printed sheet of barcodes kept in a
pocket. None was laziness. Each saved a nurse between one and four minutes a
round.

What changed. Scanners were fixed beside the medication room door, the
wristband stock was changed, and the printed sheets stopped. Scanning rose to
94% in nine months.

# Fact sheet — Aoife Brennan

Sources: `material/linkedin.md` (LinkedIn profile, saved as text, October 2026), `material/notes.md` (notes sent directly to me), `material/poster-abstract.md` (conference poster abstract, Irish Nursing Informatics Conference 2025).

## Who she is, in her own words

"Eleven years a nurse, six of them in charge of a shift. I got into informatics the night Mr D. in bed 14 nearly got another man's warfarin, because the scanner trolley was at the far end of the ward. Since then I have been the person who asks why the system makes the safe thing the slow thing." — *linkedin.md*

Part-time MSc in Health Informatics, in progress. — *linkedin.md*

**Answer:** [pending]

## Where she has been

- BSc General Nursing, Liffey University, 2011–2015. — *linkedin.md*
- Staff Nurse, Coronary Care Unit, St Brendan's University Hospital, Sep 2015–Aug 2019. — *linkedin.md*
- Clinical Nurse Manager 1, Cardiac Step-Down (28 beds), St Brendan's University Hospital, Sep 2019–present. — *linkedin.md*
- MSc Health Informatics (part-time), Liffey University, 2024–2026. — *linkedin.md*

**Answer:** [pending]

## Each job

### Staff Nurse, Coronary Care Unit (Sep 2015–Aug 2019)
No achievements or activities listed anywhere in the material. — *gap*

### CNM1, Cardiac Step-Down, 28 beds (Sep 2019–present)
- Led the redesign of the nursing handover sheet, now used on 6 wards. — *linkedin.md*
- Barcode medication scanning from 71% to 94% in 9 months. — *linkedin.md*, corroborated in detail by *poster-abstract.md*
- Preceptor to 14 newly qualified nurses. — *linkedin.md*
- Built dashboards for the falls and pressure ulcer audits. — *linkedin.md*

**Answer:** [pending]

## The title

LinkedIn headline says "Clinical Informatics Lead and CNM1, Cardiac Step-Down." Her own note says: "My manager calls me the informatics lead. On paper I am the Nursing Informatics Link Nurse, one day a week." — *notes.md*

**This is a disagreement.** The LinkedIn headline and the formal title are not the same thing, and the gap is a day of the week. — *to confirm*

**Answer:** [pending]

## The project behind the numbers: the scanning study

- On her ward, 29% of medication doses were given without scanning both wristband and medicine. — *poster-abstract.md*
- She observed for 40 hours across day and night shifts, and ran short interviews with 22 nurses. — *poster-abstract.md*
- Three workarounds accounted for most missed scans: wristbands that would not scan after a shower, scanners kept on a trolley away from the medication room, and scanning from a printed sheet of barcodes kept in a pocket. — *poster-abstract.md*
- Each workaround saved a nurse between one and four minutes a round; none was laziness. — *poster-abstract.md*
- What changed: scanners were fixed beside the medication room door, the wristband stock was changed, and the printed sheets stopped. Scanning rose to 94% in nine months. — *poster-abstract.md*
- Presented as a poster, Irish Nursing Informatics Conference 2025, single author (A. Brennan, RGN). — *poster-abstract.md*

**Answer:** [pending — whose decision was it to make these three changes, and whose to carry them out?]

## What others have said of her

Her manager calls her "the informatics lead," informally. — *notes.md*

No other quotes, references or recommendations are in the material. — *gap*

## What she learned from

The near-miss with Mr D. in bed 14, which she names as the start of her interest in informatics. — *linkedin.md*

No book, course or person is named as a source of learning, beyond the MSc itself. — *gap*

## Pictures, drawings or files she says she has

- A photo of the ward whiteboard from a night with nine admissions. "It says everything about the job." — *notes.md*. Not yet supplied as a file.
- The old handover sheet and the new one (the one she redesigned). — *notes.md*. Not yet supplied as files.

**Answer:** [pending]

## Skills

ISBAR handover, Medication safety, Audit, SQL (basic), Power BI. — *linkedin.md*

---

## Gaps

- Nothing to show for the four years as Staff Nurse, Coronary Care Unit.
- The whiteboard photo and the two handover sheets are described but not yet supplied as files.
- Nothing documenting the MSc itself — no coursework, dissertation topic, or placement.
- No picture of her, or of her presenting the poster.
- No outcome is given for the dashboards (falls, pressure ulcers) the way the scanning number has one.
- "Now used on 6 wards" has no detail on how that spread happened, or over what time.

## Disagreements

- **Title.** LinkedIn: "Clinical Informatics Lead and CNM1." Her note: formally the "Nursing Informatics Link Nurse," one day a week; "informatics lead" is what her manager calls her, not her paper title.

## To confirm

1. Which title for the site: the LinkedIn headline, the formal one-day-a-week title, or something that holds both and says so?
2. The night with Mr D. in bed 14 — a patient nearly received another patient's warfarin. May that story be told at all, and if so, with what left out (his name, the bed number, the ward)?
3. The ward whiteboard photo — did she take it, and does it show any patient's name or identifying detail?
4. The two handover sheets (old and new) — are they the hospital's property, and do they carry any patient data that would need to come out before either could be shown?
5. Is "St Brendan's University Hospital" the real name of her employer, and may it be shown on the site?
6. The scanning study (29% → 94%): was the decision to fix the three workarounds hers alone, or shared with others — and who carried out the physical changes (moving scanners, changing wristband stock)?
7. "Now used on six wards" — does she know roughly when that happened, or by whom it was carried over from her ward to the other five?
8. Anything at all to show for the four years as Staff Nurse in Coronary Care, or is Cardiac Step-Down and the MSc the whole of the story?
9. Falls and pressure ulcer dashboards — is there a result to go with them, the way scanning has 71% → 94%?

The site's spine is likely the scanning study — not because it's the biggest line on your CV, but because it's the one with a full story: a real problem, real observation, a real fix, a real number.

**Questions from the material:**

1. Title: your LinkedIn headline says "Clinical Informatics Lead and CNM1." Your note says you're formally the "Nursing Informatics Link Nurse," one day a week, and "informatics lead" is what your manager calls you. Which goes on the site — or do you want it to say both and be honest about the gap?
2. The night with Mr D. in bed 14, who nearly got another patient's warfarin — can that story be told at all, and if so, with his name and the bed number left out, or told some other way?
